record.paper_title: Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution: Protocols, Security, and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can twin-field quantum key distribution be extended from fiber links to free-space and satellite channels in a way that preserves practical secure key generation under atmospheric turbulence, beam wandering, and time-varying channel transmittance? In particular, what protocol adaptations, real-time channel-assessment methods, onboard measurement modules for low-Earth-orbit quantum satellites, and Doppler-compensation techniques are needed to support hybrid satellite-terrestrial TF-QKD networks, and how can these be validated through realistic satellite-ground experimental demonstrations?

evidence.quote: A major frontier for TF-QKD lies in extending its reach to free-space and satellite channels, thereby enabling global coverage.
Such integration requires overcoming atmospheric turbulence, beam wandering, and variable transmittance through adaptive protocols and real-time channel assessment.

Key technical challenges include designing low-Earth orbit (LEO) quantum satellites with onboard measurement modules, compensating for Doppler-induced phase fluctuations, and constructing hybrid satellite–terrestrial networks.
Experimental demonstrations of TF-QKD over realistic satellite–ground links remain a primary milestone toward practical deployment.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) is a measurement-device-independent QKD protocol in which two distant parties (Alice and Bob) each prepare phase-randomized weak coherent pulses and send them to an untrusted central node (Charlie) who performs single-photon interference detection. The asymptotic secret key rate of TF-QKD scales as O(√η), where η is the end-to-end channel transmittance, thereby beating the repeaterless PLOB bound O(η).

Existing TF-QKD implementations rely on stable optical fibers in which phase reference, channel transmittance, and timing can be tightly controlled. Extending TF-QKD to free-space and satellite-to-ground links introduces additional impairments, including: (i) atmospheric turbulence causing rapid random phase distortions of the optical wavefront, (ii) beam wandering and scintillation producing strongly time-varying transmittance η(t), (iii) Doppler shifts and Doppler-induced phase drifts arising from the relative motion between a low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite and ground stations, and (iv) the need to host the interference measurement module on a moving satellite platform with limited resources.

Develop a complete framework for free-space and satellite TF-QKD that addresses the following coupled requirements:

1. Specify a TF-QKD protocol variant (including encoding, decoy-intensity choices, and post-selection rules) whose finite-key security analysis remains valid under fluctuating transmittance η(t) and residual phase noise σφ characteristic of atmospheric and Doppler-induced fluctuations, and prove a positive secret-key-rate bound under realistic statistical models of these fluctuations.

2. Provide a real-time channel-assessment and phase-tracking method that, given measurement statistics from a satellite-borne interference detector, jointly estimates η(t) and the global phase reference with accuracy sufficient to maintain the √η scaling advantage over the PLOB bound.

3. Design an onboard LEO measurement module (optical, electronic, and synchronization specifications) compatible with the protocol of (1)–(2), and a Doppler-compensation scheme that suppresses Doppler-induced phase fluctuations below the threshold required for single-photon interference visibility.

4. Construct an architecture for hybrid satellite–terrestrial TF-QKD networks that integrates the above components, and demonstrate—through an end-to-end satellite–ground experimental implementation—a finite-key secret key rate exceeding the repeaterless PLOB bound for the satellite-to-ground channel.

The problem is to provide such a framework together with an experimental satellite–ground demonstration meeting the criteria above.
artifact.status_search_result: A first free-space TF-QKD experiment over a 14.2 km urban atmospheric channel was reported in March 2025, surpassing the effective atmospheric thickness relevant for satellite-to-ground links and beating the repeaterless capacity bound. This represents significant progress on the protocol-and-channel-assessment aspects, but a full satellite–ground TF-QKD demonstration with a LEO onboard measurement module, Doppler-compensation, and a hybrid satellite-terrestrial network architecture has not yet been achieved. The overall problem therefore remains only partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Free-Space Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution
status_evidence.snippet: First free-space TF-QKD demonstration over 14.2 km urban atmospheric channel, surpassing the effective atmospheric thickness threshold for satellite compatibility.
status_evidence.claim: Free-space TF-QKD has been experimentally demonstrated, addressing atmospheric turbulence, but not yet over a satellite-ground link.

status_evidence.title: World's first quantum microsatellite demonstrates secure communication with multiple ground stations
status_evidence.snippet: Microsatellite QKD with multiple ground stations demonstrated in 2025, but using prepare-and-measure rather than TF-QKD.
status_evidence.claim: Satellite QKD progress continues, but TF-QKD-specific satellite-to-ground demonstrations remain a milestone yet to be achieved.
